title: Engineering two-qubit gates via anisotropic exchange in germanium spin qubits
authors: Leonardo Massai, Bence Hetényi, Eoin G. Kelly, Inga Seidler, Konstantinos Tsoukalas, Michele Aldeghi, Alexei Orekhov, Lisa Sommer, Marta Pita-Vidal, Uwe von Lüpke, Stephan Paredes, Stephen W. Bedell, Felix J. Schupp, Matthias Mergenthaler, Gian Salis, Andreas Fuhrer, Patrick Harvey-Collard
abstract: Germanium hole spin qubits are a promising and versatile platform for quantum computation and simulation. In this system, strong spin-orbit interaction (SOI) renders the single-qubit $g$-tensor anisotropic and electrically tunable, enabling operational sweet spots with reduced noise sensitivity. SOI also transforms the isotropic two-qubit exchange coupling into an anisotropic tensor whose geometry is inherited from the single-qubit $g$-tensors and spin-flip tunnelling. Here, using two hole spin qubits in a strained-germanium quantum well and full vector control of the magnetic field, we map this exchange tensor, separate it into longitudinal and transverse components, and show that they govern controlled-phase and SWAP-like dynamics, respectively. We find that the longitudinal exchange can be tuned via the magnetic field orientation from a conventional positive value, through zero, to an effectively negative one, as measured by inverted exchange-split spin transitions. The magnetic field direction thus provides continuous control over the interaction Hamiltonian: at a point of purely transverse exchange, we engineer a single-pulse baseband iSWAP, unattainable under isotropic exchange. Linking $g$-tensor geometry to exchange anisotropy establishes native Hamiltonian engineering, enabling spin-based quantum simulation and gate sets selected by the global field orientation alone.
summary: The researchers engineered two-qubit gates in germanium hole spin qubits by exploiting the anisotropic nature of the exchange interaction, which arises from strong spin-orbit coupling. By controlling the external magnetic field direction, they achieved continuous tuning of the exchange Hamiltonian, enabling novel gate operations like a baseband iSWAP. This work demonstrates how material physics can be leveraged for precise quantum control in solid-state quantum computing.
main_problem: The goal is to engineer high-fidelity two-qubit quantum gates (like CPhase and iSWAP) by precisely controlling the anisotropic exchange interaction in germanium spin qubits.
main_result: They demonstrated continuous control over the exchange coupling Hamiltonian by reorienting the external magnetic field, achieving a single-pulse baseband iSWAP gate unattainable with isotropic coupling.
method: The study uses state spectroscopy (ARP) and Quantum Process Tomography (QPT) to map out the energy spectrum and characterize the fidelity of implemented quantum gates.
model_or_system: The platform is hole spin qubits in a strained-germanium quantum well. The interaction Hamiltonian is modeled as an anisotropic exchange tensor, decomposed into longitudinal ($J_{\|}$) and transverse ($J_{\perp}$) components, which are tunable by the magnetic field orientation ($\vec{B}$).
key_observables: CPhase oscillation frequency ($f_{C	ext{Phase}}$), SWAP-like oscillation frequency ($f_{	ext{SWAP}}$), coherence times ($T_2^*$, $T_H$), and process fidelity ($F_{	ext{iSWAP}}$).
important_parameters: The ability to tune the sign of the longitudinal exchange coupling ($J_{\|}$) from positive through zero to effectively negative is a key parameter control.
main_assumptions: The fidelity estimate relies on assuming depolarizing error channels and ignoring coherent error components during the SPAM sequence analysis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device structure, single-qubit g-tensors vs. B field, energy level diagrams showing $J_{\|}$ (Ising) and $J_{\perp}$ (XY) coupling, and measurements of gate fidelity via QPT/iSWAP characterization.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical system and Hamiltonian components derived from g-tensor anisotropy to measuring these couplings using spectroscopy, culminating in the demonstration and quantification of two-qubit gate fidelities.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete experimental realization of native Hamiltonian engineering in solid-state qubits, showing how material properties (g-tensors) dictate controllable quantum gates, which is highly relevant for building scalable quantum processors.
